opus-5.5.text:
I think embodiment matters a lot more than people sometimes assume, especially in the current wave where everyone is excited about scaling data and models. The physical configuration of a robot shapes what the policy actually has to learn. If you have a simple parallel-jaw gripper on a fixed arm, a lot of tasks reduce to "get the gripper to the right pose and close it." That's learnable, and you can collect a lot of data for it relatively cheaply. But it also means the policy never has to reason about things like finger coordination, contact-rich manipulation, or whole-body balance, which are exactly the things a humanoid has to deal with.

So when people talk about transferring skills from simpler robots to humanoids, I try to separate two layers. There's a more abstract layer: understanding the task, knowing which object matters, what the goal state looks like, roughly what sequence of steps you need. I think that layer transfers reasonably well across embodiments, and that's where cross-embodiment datasets and large pretrained models really help. Then there's the low-level layer: how forces are applied, how contacts are made and broken, how you recover when something slips. That layer is deeply tied to the hardware, including the kinematics, the actuators, the sensing, and even the compliance of the fingers. It doesn't transfer for free.

In my own work, a lot of what we found is that if you design the hardware and the data collection setup together, you can make learning much easier. For example, if the teleoperation interface or the data collection device matches the robot's end-effector closely, the demonstrations become much more directly usable, and the policy doesn't have to bridge a big embodiment gap. When there's a mismatch, say a human hand demonstrating for a two-finger gripper, you lose information or you introduce actions the robot physically can't reproduce.

For humanoids specifically, I think the challenge is that you're combining everything at once: dexterous hands, arms, a torso, legs, balance. The configuration space is huge, and data is still scarce. So one practical path is to learn manipulation competence on more constrained platforms, where you can iterate fast, and to think carefully about which parts of that knowledge are embodiment-agnostic. Then, on the humanoid, you invest in good data for the embodiment-specific parts, through teleoperation, simulation, or human video with careful retargeting.

I'd also say that sometimes the right answer isn't to make the learning algorithm more general, but to make the hardware a bit smarter: better tactile sensing, more forgiving compliance, form factors that make tasks naturally easier. Hardware and learning aren't separate problems. The best results usually come when you co-design them.

r001.rationale: The response separates transferable task-level understanding from embodiment-specific low-level control, including contact, forces, and recovery.

r002.rationale: It describes humanoid flexibility as contributing to a huge configuration space and added challenges, but does not say extra joints can make a task easier to perform.

r003.rationale: It says abstract knowledge may transfer from constrained platforms, but does not claim that accomplishing a highly complex task with a simple configuration signals a high likelihood of transfer.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually one of the questions I think about most, because the honest answer is that the configuration shapes everything, and it shapes it earlier than people expect.

The way I'd put it is this: a robot's body is not just the thing that executes the policy. It's part of the data distribution. If you collect demonstrations on a two-arm tabletop setup with parallel grippers, you're not just learning "how to fold a shirt." You're learning how to fold a shirt given that particular reach, that particular wrist range, that particular way the fingers close. The skill and the embodiment get entangled. So when people say "we'll learn it on a cheap platform and transfer to the humanoid," I always want to ask: what exactly do you think is being transferred?

Some things transfer pretty well. High-level task structure, the sequencing, the visual understanding of what a half-folded shirt looks like, where to grab next — that's relatively body-agnostic, and foundation models help a lot there. But the low-level stuff, the contact-rich part, is where it falls apart. A humanoid has a different center of mass, it has to stabilize its torso while it reaches, its hands may be dexterous instead of a simple gripper. The failure modes are totally different. A tabletop arm never has to worry about tipping over.

And there's a subtler thing, which is that the body determines what's easy to demonstrate. If a human teleoperates a humanoid, you get motion that's natural for a human body, which is great for a humanoid. If you teleoperate a very different configuration, the demonstrator unconsciously adapts to that robot's limits, and now your data has a bias baked in that you'd need to un-learn on the humanoid.

So my view is that you want the training embodiment to be as close as possible in the dimensions that matter for the task. Not necessarily identical — nobody can afford to collect everything on the final humanoid — but matched in hand morphology, roughly matched in workspace and kinematics. Then you can use cross-embodiment data for the parts that generalize, and keep the hard physical parts close to the real thing.

The optimistic version is that as the data gets bigger and more diverse across bodies, the model learns something like an abstract notion of "a hand that can grasp" and the embodiment gap narrows. I think that's partly true. But I don't think it ever goes to zero, because physics doesn't care about your abstraction. The humanoid still has to not fall down.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes transferable high-level task structure from embodiment-specific, contact-rich control, but it does not clearly distinguish task complexity from the difficulty of controlling the robot’s physical configuration.

r002.rationale: It notes that humanoid hands may be more dexterous, but does not state that a humanoid’s additional joint flexibility can make a task easier to perform.

r003.rationale: It says transfer depends on matching relevant physical dimensions and that the embodiment gap does not disappear; it does not claim that success on a simple configuration signals a high likelihood of humanoid transfer.

astra-6.text:
I think the robot’s physical configuration shapes both what it can learn and how it learns it. A task like picking up a cup depends on the reach of the arm, the joints in the wrist, the shape of the hand, and the feedback available through vision and touch. Some bodies make that task much easier, so what looks like better learning may partly be better mechanical design.

When you transfer that skill to a humanoid, you can often reuse the goal—where to grasp the cup, how to keep it upright—but you can’t necessarily reuse the same motor commands. The humanoid has different joint limits and dynamics, and it may need to balance while reaching. So the useful distinction is between understanding the task and controlling a particular body.

I’d want the system to learn those together, but represent them separately enough that a new body doesn’t mean starting from zero. Training across different configurations could help it learn what stays consistent, while experience on the humanoid teaches it how to execute the skill with its own physical constraints.

r001.rationale: It separates understanding the task from controlling a particular body and explains how body mechanics affect performance.

r002.rationale: It mentions the humanoid’s different joint limits, but does not say its greater joint flexibility can make the task easier.

r003.rationale: It discusses reusing task goals across bodies, but does not claim that mastering a complex task with a simple configuration predicts likely transfer to a humanoid.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the physical configuration is part of the learning problem. Where the joints are, how far the arms can reach, how the hands make contact, and how the robot balances all determine which strategies it can discover. A task that is straightforward for one body might be very difficult for another, even if they use the same learning algorithm.

For transfer to a humanoid, I would separate the intent of the task from the motion used to achieve it. “Pick up the cup and place it on the table” can transfer, but the exact joint trajectories usually cannot. The humanoid needs to translate that intent into movements that respect its own reach, balance, and contact constraints.

So a similar physical configuration helps, especially for manipulation and whole-body tasks, but similarity alone isn’t enough. You want training that exposes the policy to variation in the body and its dynamics, and then some adaptation on the target robot. The goal is to learn what matters about the task while still understanding what this particular body can do.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a task’s difficulty from how difficult it is for a particular body to perform, noting that the same task may be straightforward for one body and difficult for another.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a humanoid’s additional joint flexibility can make a task easier.

r003.rationale: It does not argue that success with a simple configuration on a highly complex task predicts a high likelihood of transfer to a humanoid; it instead discusses body similarity, variation, and adaptation.
